items.stem: A server has 4,000 MB of RAM. The operating system, nginx and the database already use 1,000 MB. You want to keep 15% of the RAM free, and each worker needs 200 MB. About how many workers can you run?

options.feedback: Keeping 15% free leaves 3,400 MB. Taking away the 1,000 MB already in use leaves 2,400 MB, and 2,400 divided by 200 is 12.
This divides 3,000 MB by 200 and forgets the 15% that should stay free. Without free memory the machine slows down.
This divides 3,400 MB by 200 and forgets that the operating system, nginx and the database already use 1,000 MB.
This divides all 4,000 MB by 200. Part of the RAM is already in use before the first worker starts.

items.stem: An application spends most of each request waiting for the database. You want it to handle more requests at once without a large rise in memory. What is a reasonable step?

options.text: Run several threads inside each worker, since threads share the worker's memory.
options.feedback: Threads in one process share its memory, so they cost little extra. While one thread waits for the database, another can run.

options.text: Start many more workers, since each worker handles another request.
options.feedback: This works, but each new worker is a separate process with its own copy of the application. The memory cost is large.

options.text: Do nothing, because a worker can only ever handle one request at a time.
options.feedback: A worker with several threads can overlap its waiting. Only running Python code in two threads at the same moment is blocked.

items.stem: The application machine already has plenty of free RAM, and its workers have all the memory they need. Which reason still supports moving Postgres to its own machine?

options.text: The database can be backed up and restarted without affecting the application.
options.feedback: Separate machines can be maintained separately, and a runaway query cannot use up the application's memory. These reasons do not depend on spare RAM.

options.text: Queries become faster, because a network is quicker than the same machine.
options.feedback: A query that crosses a network takes longer, about 0.4 ms more in this model. It never gets faster than a query inside the machine.

options.text: The monthly cost goes down, because each of the two machines is smaller.
options.feedback: Two machines cost about twice as much as one in this model.

options.text: More workers will fit on the application machine, which adds capacity.
options.feedback: This only helps when memory was the limit. Here the application machine already has free RAM.

items.stem: The machine has 16 GB of RAM, so the workers have plenty of memory. Does moving Postgres to its own machine lower the cost per request per second?

options.text: Yes, because the database gets a whole machine to itself.
options.feedback: A faster database helps a little, but the cost doubles. The workers were not short of memory, so throughput grows only slightly.

options.text: No, the cost per request per second goes up.
options.feedback: The second machine doubles the monthly cost, and throughput rises by only a small amount in the model. The cost for each request per second therefore goes up.

options.text: It stays the same, because the total RAM is the same.
options.feedback: The total RAM doubles, because the database gets its own 16 GB machine, and the monthly cost doubles with it.

items.try: Go to the step "Move the database to its own machine", set Total RAM to 16 GB and read the bottom row of the table.
